questions.q: The normal serum phosphorus range used in this chapter is ___ mg/dL.
questions.exp: The page gives 2.5–4.5 mg/dL; values above 4.5 are classified as hyperphosphatemia. (Book p887)

questions.q: A stable patient has phosphate 1.8 mg/dL without symptoms. How does the opening severity diagram classify this value?
questions.exp: The 1–2.5 mg/dL branch is described as asymptomatic without routine treatment in this simplified diagram. Later pages discuss oral replacement; decisions depend on cause and clinical context. (Book p887)

questions.q: Which phosphate level crosses the chapter's severe-depletion threshold rather than merely its low-reference threshold?
questions.exp: The severe phosphorus-depletion branch is <1 mg/dL. (Book p887)

questions.q: Assess: I Most body phosphorus is in the inorganic extracellular pool. II Routine serum phosphorus predominantly measures inorganic extracellular phosphate.
questions.exp: The forms tree separates the larger organic intracellular pool from inorganic HPO4 in extracellular blood, the pool measured in serum assays. (Book p887)

questions.q: Match the following phosphorus compartments — 1) Bone 2) Soft tissue 3) Extracellular fluid … A) 85% B) 14% C) 1%
questions.exp: The phosphorus column allocates 85% to bone, 14% to soft tissue and 1% to ECF. (Book p887)

questions.q: Total body stores in the comparison table are about ___ calcium versus ___ phosphorus.
questions.exp: The table contrasts approximately 1200 g of calcium with 500–800 g of phosphorus. (Book p887)

questions.q: Match the following calcium compartments — 1) Bone 2) Soft tissue 3) ECF … A) 99.3% B) 0.6% C) 0.1%
questions.exp: The calcium distribution is 99.3% bone, 0.6% soft tissue and 0.1% extracellular, distinct from the phosphate distribution. (Book p887)

questions.q: Albumin falls in a patient whose calcium and phosphate are both measured. Which correction approach follows the comparison table?
opts: Apply the same albumin correction to both minerals
Correct phosphate only because its binding is greater
Ignore albumin because both minerals are entirely free
Consider calcium correction; do not use a corrected-phosphate formula
questions.exp: The table gives 40% albumin binding for calcium versus 10% for phosphorus and states there is no role for corrected phosphorus. (Book p887)

questions.q: Albumin-bound fractions are approximately ___ for calcium and ___ for phosphorus.
questions.exp: These fractions explain why albumin correction is discussed for calcium but not routinely for phosphate. (Book p887)

questions.q: Match the following — 1) Main calcium/phosphate absorption site in the source 2) Magnesium absorption site 3) Calcium absorption protein … A) Jejunum B) Ileum C) Calbindin
questions.exp: The page groups calcium and phosphate with jejunal absorption, names the ileum for magnesium and includes calbindin in calcium handling. (Book p887)

questions.q: The net intestinal absorption fractions in the comparison are calcium ___ and phosphorus ___.
questions.exp: The table shows 20% net calcium absorption and 60% net phosphorus absorption. (Book p887)

questions.q: Evaluate: I The source splits phosphate absorption into 80% active and 20% passive. II It splits calcium absorption into 95% active and 5% passive.
questions.exp: These are the chapter's contrasting active/passive fractions; the active phosphate arm is labeled vitamin-D dependent. (Book p887)

questions.q: A student says the page's shared absorption sketch proves that calbindin transports phosphate directly. Which correction is most appropriate?
opts: Vitamin D promotes both; calbindin specifically supports calcium handling
Calbindin is the principal renal phosphate cotransporter
Phosphate is absorbed only by passive diffusion
Vitamin D has no intestinal phosphate effect
questions.exp: The schematic groups vitamin D and the two minerals, but calbindin should not be misidentified as the sodium–phosphate transporter. It is a calcium-binding protein, not vitamin-D-binding protein despite the handwritten label. (Book p887)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: Proximal phosphate reclamation uses the ___ cotransporters and is powered by ___.
questions.exp: The page names sodium–phosphate cotransporters IIa and IIc in the PCT and labels transport secondary active. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: Which model best describes proximal tubular phosphate handling?
opts: Minor uptake with most recovery by collecting-duct NaPi
Major NaPi-mediated uptake regulated by PTH and FGF23
Fixed 99% uptake unaffected by PTH or FGF23
Predominantly paracellular uptake regulated by calcitonin
questions.exp: The PCT is the major regulated site, but the printed 99% should not be taught as an invariant filtered-load reabsorption fraction. Hormones and intake change renal phosphate handling. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: A child with glucosuria despite normal glucose, proximal bicarbonate wasting and severe rickets has which phosphate mechanism?
opts: Autonomous calcitriol excess causing phosphate retention
Absent PTH causing increased proximal phosphate uptake
Generalized proximal dysfunction causing phosphate wasting
Isolated distal acidification failure causing phosphate retention
questions.exp: Fanconi syndrome involves generalized PCT dysfunction, phosphate depletion and severe mineralization defects. Isolated type II RTA need not imply the full Fanconi syndrome. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: An early-CKD patient still has a normal serum phosphate despite declining filtration. Which compensation explains this?
opts: Loss of every renal Klotho receptor
FGF23 suppression of proximal NaPi transport
FGF23 activation of proximal NaPi transport
questions.exp: FGF23 reduces NaPi transport, increases phosphaturia and can maintain normal serum phosphate early in CKD. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: FGF23 inhibits renal ___, reducing calcitriol-mediated calcium absorption and contributing to secondary HPT.
questions.exp: The diagram connects FGF23 inhibition of 1α-hydroxylase to lower calcium absorption and secondary hyperparathyroidism. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: Assess: I High phosphate in advanced CKD proves FGF23 concentrations are low. II The source attributes reduced FGF23 effectiveness to impaired Klotho signaling.
questions.exp: The source calls this 'FGF23 inactivated' due to Klotho resistance; this is impaired effectiveness, not evidence that circulating FGF23 concentrations are low. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: Match the following vascular concepts — 1) CKD phosphate-associated calcification 2) Atherosclerotic calcification 3) Mineralizing vascular-cell phenotype … A) Medial B) Intimal C) Osteoblast-like
questions.exp: The source contrasts medial calcification in CKD with intimal calcification in atherosclerosis and depicts osteogenic transformation of vascular cells. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: An advanced-CKD diagram ends with 'unfit for renal transplant' after medial calcification. How should this endpoint be interpreted clinically?
opts: Evidence that phosphate must be low before evaluation begins
Proof that atherosclerotic calcification is always medial
A simplified warning requiring individualized vascular assessment
An automatic permanent exclusion for every calcified vessel
questions.exp: Severe vascular calcification can complicate transplant suitability, but the diagram's categorical endpoint is not a universal eligibility rule. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: Match the following net mineral effects — 1) PTH 2) Vitamin D 3) FGF23 … A) Raises Ca, lowers phosphate B) Promotes phosphate excretion C) Raises Ca and phosphate
questions.exp: PTH raises calcium while promoting phosphaturia; vitamin D raises absorption of both; FGF23 promotes phosphate excretion. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: Evaluate the feedback notes: I PTH promotes vitamin D activation, and vitamin D stimulates FGF23. II FGF23 normally inhibits PTH and active-vitamin-D production.
questions.exp: The notes depict PTH → vitamin D → FGF23 stimulation, with FGF23 negative feedback on PTH and vitamin D; resistance can modify this in CKD. (Book p888)

questions.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
questions.q: The two bone-cell products named at the bottom of the page are ___ and ___.
questions.exp: The source groups FGF23 and sclerostin under osteoblast secretion. More precisely, osteocytes are important sources, particularly for sclerostin. (Book p888)

questions.q: A patient with renal failure develops a high phosphate and tingling with carpopedal spasm. Which link explains the neuromuscular features?
questions.exp: Hyperphosphatemia may present with hypocalcemic symptoms and vascular medial calcification because phosphate complexes calcium. (Book p889)

questions.q: Match the following hyperphosphatemia mechanisms — 1) Phosphate enema 2) CKD 3) Tumor lysis … A) Excess intake B) Reduced excretion C) Intracellular release
questions.exp: The page's first three cause groups are increased intake, reduced renal excretion and redistribution from cells to blood. (Book p889)

questions.q: The common intake-related trigger singled out for hyperphosphatemia is a phosphate-containing ___.
questions.exp: Phosphate-containing enemas can deliver an important phosphate load, especially when renal clearance is impaired. (Book p889)

questions.q: After chemotherapy, potassium and phosphate rise while calcium falls. Which process most directly explains the phosphate change?
opts: Increased proximal reabsorption from low FGF23 alone
questions.exp: Tumor lysis releases intracellular potassium, phosphate and magnesium; released phosphate complexes calcium. (Book p889)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out for the cell-to-blood phosphate redistribution group?
questions.exp: Insulin shifts phosphate into cells and can lower serum phosphate. The other options appear in the high-phosphate redistribution group. (Book p889)

questions.q: Assess: I Both respiratory and metabolic alkalosis are listed as cell-to-blood phosphate-release causes. II Elevated phosphate necessarily reflects dietary excess.
questions.exp: The listed acid-base causes are respiratory or metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis. Renal retention and cellular release also raise phosphate without dietary excess. (Book p889)

questions.q: Match the following phosphate-raising settings — 1) Lymphoma 2) Renal failure 3) Massive muscle injury … A) Cellular release B) Increased calcitriol pathway C) Reduced clearance
questions.exp: The cause tree places lymphoma with 1α-hydroxylase-associated conditions, renal failure under impaired excretion and rhabdomyolysis under redistribution. (Book p889)

questions.q: Which condition is not in the chapter's 1α-hydroxylase-associated hyperphosphatemia group?
questions.exp: The source groups acromegaly, lymphoma, sarcoid cells and granulomas with increased calcitriol-related phosphate absorption. Fanconi syndrome instead wastes phosphate. (Book p889)

questions.q: A young patient has slowly growing periarticular calcific soft-tissue masses and high phosphate. A recessive FGF23 loss-of-function defect is found. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.exp: Loss of FGF23 action impairs phosphate excretion, promoting calcium–phosphate masses in familial tumoral calcinosis. (Book p889)

questions.q: The inheritance and FGF23 functional change specified for familial tumoral calcinosis are ___ and ___.
questions.exp: The source specifies an autosomal-recessive missense loss-of-function FGF23 variant for this form of tumoral calcinosis. (Book p889)

questions.q: Evaluate: I The page names the knee as the common periarticular site of tumoral calcinosis. II The hand radiograph is an example of soft-tissue calcification rather than proof that the hand is the commonest site.
questions.exp: The text emphasizes the knee and slow-growing tumor-like soft-tissue masses; the illustration shows calcification in a hand. (Book p889)

questions.q: A hyperphosphatemic patient already has high serum calcium. Which listed binder avoids adding a calcium load?
questions.exp: The page favors non-calcium phosphate binders, including sevelamer, ferric citrate and sucroferric oxyhydroxide, because calcium-containing binders may worsen hypercalcemia. (Book p889)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out among the non-calcium phosphate binders listed?
questions.exp: Calcium acetate supplies calcium; the three listed non-calcium alternatives do not. (Book p889)

questions.q: A dialysis-dependent patient has severe persistent hyperphosphatemia despite dietary restriction and binders. Which removal method does the page call the best?
questions.exp: Dialysis is listed as the best removal method in this context, alongside intake restriction and attention to associated hypocalcemia. (Book p890)

questions.q: Which proposed diet change conflicts with the chapter's hyperphosphatemia advice?
questions.exp: The restriction list includes dairy products, pickles, nuts, chocolate and dates; increasing dairy and nuts goes against it. (Book p890)

questions.q: Assess: I Management includes attention to associated hypocalcemia. II Every asymptomatic low calcium during phosphate excess requires aggressive calcium loading.
questions.exp: The page says to treat associated hypocalcemia, but aggressive calcium loading can increase calcium–phosphate precipitation; severity and symptoms guide clinical treatment. (Book p890)

questions.q: The clinical-feature list for severe hypophosphatemia is introduced at serum phosphate below ___ mg/dL.
questions.exp: The page associates clinically significant depletion with phosphate <1 mg/dL. (Book p890)

questions.q: Match the following depletion effects — 1) RBC 2) Cardiac muscle 3) Proximal skeletal muscle … A) Hemolysis B) Myopathy C) Cardiomyopathy
questions.exp: The feature list includes RBC hemolysis, cardiomyopathy and proximal myopathy, as well as growth retardation and rhabdomyolysis. (Book p890)

questions.q: Which is the odd one out among the listed severe phosphate-depletion consequences?
questions.exp: Calcific masses belong to phosphate excess/tumoral calcinosis, unlike the depletion features listed here. (Book p890)

questions.q: A malnourished patient with phosphate 0.6 mg/dL develops rhabdomyolysis; phosphate then rises as muscle breaks down. Which explanation reconciles this sequence?
opts: The initial low value rules out a causal role for depletion
Both measurements must be laboratory errors
Depletion predisposes to injury; cell lysis subsequently releases phosphate
Rhabdomyolysis can only occur after phosphate excess
questions.exp: The note explicitly distinguishes low phosphate as a risk factor from high phosphate resulting from muscle-cell release after rhabdomyolysis. (Book p890)

questions.q: Evaluate the source's vitamin-D note: I Severe deficiency can lower phosphate. II Every mild vitamin-D deficiency must produce severe phosphate depletion.
questions.exp: The note emphasizes severe vitamin-D deficiency and severe hypocalcemia, rather than claiming that all lesser deficiencies cause profound hypophosphatemia. (Book p890)

questions.q: During treatment of DKA, phosphate falls after insulin begins. Which mechanism best fits?
questions.exp: Insulin after DKA is listed among blood-to-cell redistribution causes; this differs from cellular destruction. (Book p890)

questions.q: The most characteristic metabolic abnormality named for refeeding syndrome is ___.
questions.exp: The page identifies low phosphate as the most common metabolic abnormality of refeeding. (Book p890)

questions.q: Match the following low-phosphate mechanisms — 1) Nutritional rickets 2) Refeeding 3) Hungry bone syndrome … A) Insulin-associated intracellular shift B) Increased skeletal mineral uptake C) Reduced nutrient/vitamin-D supply
questions.exp: The source separates reduced intake from redistribution; hungry bone directs minerals into bone, while refeeding drives cellular uptake. (Book p890)

questions.q: Which does not belong in the page's hypophosphatemic redistribution list?
questions.exp: Sepsis, heat stroke and hyperthermia are listed with redistribution causes; FGF23 loss impairs phosphate excretion and favors hyperphosphatemia. (Book p890)

questions.q: In the sepsis note, evaluate: I The phosphate fall is emphasized more than the calcium fall. II The shorthand excludes coexisting hypophosphatemia.
questions.exp: The shorthand is '↓Ca > ↓P': a relative emphasis, not exclusion of hypophosphatemia. (Book p890)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: Match the following hypophosphatemic-rickets inheritance patterns — 1) X-linked 2) Autosomal recessive 3) Autosomal dominant … A) DMP1 B) PHEX C) FGF23
questions.exp: The source lists PHEX for the common X-linked form, DMP (DMP1) for a recessive form and FGF23 for the dominant form. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: A family has phosphate-wasting rickets with an X-linked pattern. Which gene is the best match to the chapter's commonest inherited form?
questions.exp: PHEX-related disease is the most common inherited hypophosphatemic rickets form named in the table. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: An FGF23 variant resists proteolytic cleavage. Which combination of intact FGF23 action and serum phosphate is expected?
questions.exp: The later laboratory note correctly links phosphate wasting to increased FGF23 activity. The table's downward arrow should be treated as an error, and PHEX/DMP1 regulation is more complex than direct cleavage alone. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: Match the following typical rickets laboratory findings — 1) Serum phosphate 2) ALP 3) Calcium and PTH … A) Raised B) Usually normal C) Low
questions.exp: The page lists low phosphate, increased ALP and normal calcium/PTH in inherited hypophosphatemic rickets. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: A child has lower-limb deformity, low phosphate, high ALP and normal calcium and PTH. Which disorder best fits?
questions.exp: Lower-limb-predominant rickets with isolated phosphate wasting matches the source phenotype, rather than a primary calcium/PTH disorder. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: Which is the odd one out among causes of renal phosphate wasting on this page?
questions.exp: The renal causes include proximal tubular dysfunction/type II RTA, inherited rickets and tubular injury; loss of FGF23 action promotes phosphate retention. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: An adult develops bone pain, weakness and phosphate wasting from a mesenchymal tumor. What is the best mechanistic explanation?
opts: Suppressed proximal phosphate transport from absent PTH
questions.exp: Tumor-induced osteomalacia is typically due to FGF23 secretion by a mesenchymal tumor. The source's 'gain-of-function mutation' shorthand should not imply that such a mutation is required in every case. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: The source's daily phosphorus requirement entry is ___, while each listed Adphos tablet is ___.
questions.exp: The page prints a 2 g daily requirement and 250 mg Adphos tablets; the requirement is a source-specific teaching value, not a universal dietary recommendation. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: Using the page's low-fat-milk phosphate concentration of 0.9 mg/mL, 250 mL provides approximately ___ mg.
questions.exp: 0.9 × 250 = 225 mg. Low-fat milk is listed as an oral source for mild depletion. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: Match the following replacement entries — 1) Mild depletion 2) Severe depletion 3) Dietary source … A) IV phosphorus B) Oral phosphate tablets C) Low-fat milk
questions.exp: The chapter separates oral replacement for mild disease from IV replacement for severe disease and also lists low-fat milk. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: Which IV phosphorus regimen is printed for severe hypophosphatemia?
questions.exp: The source gives 10 mg/kg over 12 hours. Actual IV phosphate prescribing requires a validated preparation-specific protocol, renal assessment and calcium/phosphate monitoring. (Book p891)

questions.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
questions.q: Compare the mild-phosphate entries: I The opening diagram labels asymptomatic 1–2.5 mg/dL as not needing treatment. II The final page discusses oral replacement for mild disease.
questions.exp: Both statements occur in the source. They should not be collapsed into a universal treat-all or treat-none rule. (Book p891)

units.title: Phosphorus: ranges, compartments and absorption
units.sec: Phosphorus: ranges, compartments and absorption · p887
units.guide: Compare Ca and phosphate stores, albumin binding and intestinal fractions. Serum phosphate assays measure inorganic extracellular phosphate; do not apply the calcium correction formula to phosphate.

units.title: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis
units.sec: Renal phosphate and the FGF23–Klotho axis · p888
units.guide: Follow PCT transport through Fanconi syndrome, compensatory phosphaturia in early CKD and impaired signaling in advanced CKD. Distinguish medial vascular calcification from atherosclerotic intimal calcification.

units.title: Hyperphosphatemia: causes, calcinosis and binders
units.sec: Hyperphosphatemia: causes, calcinosis and binders · p889
units.guide: Trace increased intake, reduced excretion, cell release and calcitriol-driven absorption. Familial tumoral calcinosis is contrasted with phosphate-wasting FGF23 disorders. Prefer non-calcium binders when calcium loading is a concern.

units.title: Phosphate removal, depletion and redistribution
units.sec: Phosphate removal, depletion and redistribution · p890
units.guide: Diet and dialysis address phosphate excess. Severe depletion affects growth, RBCs, skeletal and cardiac muscle and insulin sensitivity. Understand the two directions linking phosphate and rhabdomyolysis.

units.title: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement
units.sec: Phosphate wasting, inherited rickets and replacement · p891
units.guide: Read inheritance and gene pairs, then the common biochemical phenotype. The table contains a reversed FGF23 arrow: reduced cleavage must not be taught as low active FGF23. Tumor-induced osteomalacia reflects excess tumor-derived FGF23, not a mandatory germline mutation.
